claims.text: Integrating ultrafast scanning calorimetry, in-situ neutron imaging, and CALPHAD analysis provides an accurate route for determining HEA melting properties.
The integrated method is efficient across diverse HEA compositions.
Single-phase HEAs can occur as FCC or BCC solid solutions.
Ultrafast DSC can determine melting temperature and fusion enthalpy in HEAs.
Real-time neutron imaging can track microstructural evolution and the melting front during HEA fusion.
CALPHAD-guided analysis can extract liquid-phase thermodynamic properties from the coupled measurements.
High heating rates suppress kinetic delays during melting.
A liquid-solid interface during fusion will produce distinct neutron-attenuation changes that coincide with DSC heat-flow peaks.
Rapid heating minimizes non-equilibrium effects and phase segregation.
In-situ neutron imaging enables direct correlation of calorimetric signals with structural changes during melting.
CALPHAD phase-behavior baselines improve extraction of fusion enthalpy and entropy.
The combined method can determine volume change at HEA melting.
Measured melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change will agree with CALPHAD predictions within 5–10%.
Fusion properties will vary systematically with composition across the HEA family.
Standard DSC or ex-situ thermal analysis often gives less accurate thermodynamic estimates because it does not account for rapid structural evolution or kinetic effects.
The method is most applicable to HEAs with relatively simple single-phase behavior before melting.
Multiphase or metastable HEAs may require additional analytical corrections.
Refractory HEAs and alloys with complex melting behavior may require additional calibration.
